summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors, and Central Kalimantan stands under that national framework. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Central Kalimantan has no equivalent provincial criminalisation.

Physical risk is rising nationally. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue; on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor and arrested 75 people, and Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested on drug charges and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, and Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
OutRight Action International's 2022 report 'Creeping Criminalisation' maps national laws and regional regulations in Indonesia that violate the rights of women and LGBTIQ people. Its list of eight provinces with discriminatory regional regulations does not include Central Kalimantan, indicating that the province has not adopted the kind of local morality ordinances seen elsewhere in Indonesia.

The absence of a Central Kalimantan-specific regulation does not reduce the national exposure a visitor faces: the 2023 penal code, the 2006 pornography law, and the October 2025 presidential decree on national threats apply throughout the country, including in this province.
localsOnly:
Indonesia's 2023 Penal Code (RUU KUHP) was passed on 6 December 2022 and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after enactment. It criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if an immediate family member lodges a complaint. The code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under the outside-marriage restriction.

Legal gender recognition in Indonesia requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and identity documents carry only 'male' or 'female' markers. There is no national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents of Central Kalimantan have no statutory remedy for orientation- or identity-based harassment.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Central Kalimantan provincial authorities have conducted raids, prosecutions, or vigilante incidents targeting trans people is not sourced in this inventory; the available evidence addresses the national framework and other provinces. The claim that prosecutions under the 2026 penal code are selective rather than systematic rests on reporting rather than case-level data, and the number of actual prosecutions since 2 January 2026 remains unresolved.

The status and fate of the 2025 bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour is not sourced beyond its being under discussion in 2025; whether it has since been enacted is unresolved here.
